content: If the goal is to achieve a meaningful and lasting impact, certain components of an implementation strategy can be considered optional. However, the strategy itself is designed to be flexible and adaptable without compromising its integrity or intended outcomes. Depending on the local context and available resources, some elements may be emphasized more than others or implemented in different ways. Regular assessments allow healthcare facilities to focus their efforts on all, some, or just one of the components at any given time. In Section II, we examined another implementation model, the Four E’s (engage, educate, execute, and evaluate), which outlines critical success factors for improvement programs. This model was used to review literature on interventions aimed at improving surgical practices and reducing surgical site infections (SSIs). Both this approach and the WHO multimodal strategy share a common focus on how improvement programs can be effectively organized to support and enable the implementation of technical prevention measures, such as protocols for the proper insertion and maintenance of central-line catheters. These frameworks provide the foundation for creating an environment conducive to organizational and behavioral change across teams and within specific settings. The aim of these strategies is to promote a consistent global approach that facilitates the adaptation and implementation of infection prevention and control (IPC) guidelines into practice. There is clear alignment and synergy between the two proven approaches, even when this is not immediately apparent due to differences in terminology. In summary, system change involves executing the right actions in the right place at the right time. Training and education align with the educate component of the Four E’s model, while evaluation and feedback correspond to engage and evaluate. Workplace reminders and communication foster engagement, and institutional safety culture or climate change underpins all components of the Four E’s. The relevance of applying the WHO multimodal strategy for SSI prevention aligns well with existing evidence supporting the efficacy of the Four E’s model. The multimodal approach to SSI prevention is structured around five components, which describe how healthcare facilities can apply this strategy in their local context and translate recommendations into practice. However, it is important to note that this is not a practical manual for implementing an SSI improvement program. The work required to prepare the entire facility for the necessary interventions or changes should not be underestimated, as this is critical for success and reflects the facility’s culture of improvement and commitment to safe, high-quality care. The five-step cycle of improvement to support IPC intervention implementation includes the following: 1. System Change: Ensure the facility has the necessary infrastructure and resources to implement and sustain the recommendations. This involves assessing the current system and identifying limitations that hinder the implementation of SSI prevention measures. For example, the procurement of specific equipment may be required. Other key measures, such as sterilization of surgical instruments, may also necessitate system changes. The right infrastructure and resources streamline interventions, ensuring consistent and safe care delivery. 2. Training and Education: Effective and practical training methods aligned with evidence-based SSI prevention recommendations are essential. Training empowers healthcare workers and ensures that education remains a constant in healthcare quality and safety. It should target all disciplines involved in patient care and be tailored to engage the audience, helping them understand how required changes fit within their clinical workflow. 3. Baseline Assessment: Conduct an initial evaluation to identify gaps in current practices and detect strengths, such as champions who can advocate for the recommendations. 4. Developing and Executing the Plan: Create a detailed action plan for implementing the necessary changes, including timelines and specific roles and responsibilities. 5. Evaluating Impact and Sustaining the Program: Regularly assess the outcomes of the implemented changes and establish mechanisms to ensure the program’s long-term sustainability. Examples of WHO SSI prevention recommendations requiring system change include: Preoperative intranasal application of mupirocin 2% ointment for patients with known nasal carriage of Staphylococcus aureus, with or without chlorhexidine gluconate body wash. Administration of surgical antibiotic prophylaxis (SAP) before the surgical incision, ensuring it is delivered at the right time and place. Proper surgical hand preparation using either antimicrobial soap and water or alcohol-based hand rub before donning sterile gloves. Use of alcohol-based antiseptic solutions containing chlorhexidine gluconate for surgical site skin preparation. Avoidance of hair removal unless absolutely necessary, and if required, using clippers instead of razors. Consideration of oral or enteral multiple nutrient-enhanced nutritional formulas for underweight patients undergoing major surgery. Use of warming devices during surgery to maintain patient body temperature and reduce SSI risk. Implementation of intensive perioperative blood glucose control protocols for diabetic and non-diabetic patients. Use of goal-directed fluid therapy intraoperatively to reduce SSI risk. Selection of sterile, disposable non-woven or reusable woven drapes and surgical gowns during operations. Irrigation of the incisional wound with aqueous povidone-iodine solution before closure, particularly for clean and clean-contaminated wounds. Administration of 80% inspired oxygen intraoperatively and postoperatively for patients under general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation. Avoidance of advanced dressings over standard dressings on primarily closed surgical wounds. To implement these recommendations effectively, healthcare facilities must address infrastructure and resource needs, secure budgets, and develop action plans with clear roles and responsibilities. Facilities should also establish systems for ongoing monitoring and feedback, update documentation, and ensure the availability of valid tools to support system changes. Additionally, training and education should be tailored to engage healthcare workers and integrate required changes into their clinical workflows.
